big: Meena bought a fund at ₹100 a unit. It fell to ₹70. She says, 'I will sell only when it gets back to ₹100.' Her money has been stuck for two years. The price she paid is not a reason to hold.

lines: I cannot sell below what I paid. It feels like admitting a mistake.
That is anchoring. The first number sticks in the mind. A better question: if I had this money in cash today, would I buy this fund? If not, why hold it?

rows: A low NAV is not cheap
note: NAV is just the value of one unit. It tells you nothing about whether the fund is good value.

title: Anchoring and NAV
stops: Anchoring means a first number sticks in the mind
A fund with NAV ₹10 is cheaper than ₹100
Break-even thinking can trap money in a poor fund
Selling below your cost is always a mistake
caps: A price paid becomes the number we cannot let go.
NAV is value per unit and says nothing about value.
Waiting to get even can lock money in a poor choice.
Judge by today's facts, not by what you paid.

q: Rohan will sell a fund only when it returns to the ₹100 he paid. What is this?
why: Diversification is spreading money, which he is not doing.
Rebalancing is returning to a target mix.
He is stuck on the first number, his purchase price.
A stop-loss is an order, which he has not placed.

q: A new fund has a NAV of ₹10 and an older fund a NAV of ₹100. Which is cheaper?
opts: Neither, NAV is just per unit
The one with a much nicer name
why: NAV is value per unit and says nothing about price.
A lower NAV gives more units, not more value.
A higher NAV gives fewer units, not less value.
A name has no link to value, so it does not matter.

q: Which question helps Meena escape break-even thinking?
opts: What price did I pay for it?
What does my neighbour think of it?
Will it ever return to ₹100 again?
Would I buy it today with cash?
why: The price paid is the anchor, so it keeps her stuck.
A neighbour's view is not a test of the fund's fit.
Hoping for a return to ₹100 is the trap itself.
It judges the fund by today's facts, not by her price.

q: Rohan puts ₹10,000 in a ₹10 NAV fund and ₹10,000 in a ₹100 NAV fund. Both rise 10%. What are they worth?
why: The NAV level does not change the percentage gain.
Each has ₹10,000 growing 10%, so each becomes ₹11,000.
The ₹10 fund does not double. It rises by the same 10%.
These numbers confuse units with rupees.

pts: Anchoring: the first number, such as the price paid, sticks in the mind.
A ₹10 NAV is not cheaper than a ₹100 NAV.
Ask: would I buy this today with cash? If not, why hold it?
